arXiv:2609.21905v1 [math.OC] 18 Sep 2026

An Ω⁡(κy8​ϵ−6)\Omega(\kappa_{y}^{8}\epsilon^{-6}) Lower Bound for Stochastic NC-SC Bilevel Optimization with First-order Oracles

Zhihao Gu The Pennsylvania State University zbg5155@psu.edu Qilong Wu The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen qilongwu@link.cuhk.edu.cn Junchi Yang† The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen yangjunchi@cuhk.edu.cn
Abstract

We study the oracle complexity of finding ϵ\epsilon-stationary points of smooth bilevel optimization problems with a nonconvex upper-level objective and a strongly convex lower-level problem. We consider a stochastic first-order oracle that returns unbiased stochastic gradients of both the upper- and lower-level objectives, with variance bounded by σ2\sigma^{2}. We prove that, for any initial optimality gap Δ>0\Delta>0 and all sufficiently small ϵ>0\epsilon>0, every adaptive randomized first-order algorithm requires Ω⁡(Δ​κy2​ϵ−2​max⁡{1,σ2​κy6​ϵ−4})\Omega\!\left(\Delta\kappa_{y}^{2}\epsilon^{-2}\max\{1,\sigma^{2}\kappa_{y}^{6}\epsilon^{-4}\}\right) oracle queries to find an ϵ\epsilon-stationary point of its hyper-objective function, where κy\kappa_{y} denotes the condition number of the lower-level problem. In particular, in the noise-dominated regime, the lower bound is Ω⁡(Δ​σ2​κy8​ϵ−6).\Omega\!\left(\Delta\sigma^{2}\kappa_{y}^{8}\epsilon^{-6}\right). This establishes the optimality of the ϵ−6\epsilon^{-6} dependence achieved by the best-known first-order stochastic methods.

1 Introduction

Bilevel optimization is a fundamental framework for hierarchical decision making in which one optimization problem is nested inside another (Colson et al., 2007). In its canonical unconstrained form, the problem is written as

min𝒙∈ℝdx⁡Φ⁡(𝒙)≔f⁡(𝒙,𝒚∗​(𝒙)),𝒚∗​(𝒙)≔arg⁡min𝒚∈ℝdy⁡g⁡(𝒙,𝒚).\min_{\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}}\Phi(\bm{x})\coloneqq f\bigl(\bm{x},\bm{y}^{*}(\bm{x})\bigr),\qquad\bm{y}^{*}(\bm{x})\coloneqq\arg\min_{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}}g(\bm{x},\bm{y}). (1)

This nested structure captures a wide range of modern learning problems, including hyperparameter optimization and meta-learning (Franceschi et al., 2018; Rajeswaran et al., 2019), as well as reinforcement learning and actor-critic methods (Hong et al., 2023).

We study the smooth nonconvex-strongly-convex setting, where g⁡(𝒙,⋅)g(\bm{x},\cdot) is strongly convex for every 𝒙\bm{x}, while the upper-level objective ff, and hence the hyper-objective Φ\Phi, may be nonconvex. Under standard smoothness assumptions, Φ\Phi is differentiable, but its gradient involves the inverse lower-level Hessian. Classical approaches therefore approximate this inverse (Ghadimi and Wang, 2018; Ji et al., 2021), typically requiring Hessian-vector and thus access to second-order information. Since such products can be substantially more expensive than gradients, first-order bilevel methods using only upper- and lower-level gradients have been developed (Shen and Chen, 2023; Kwon et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025b; Kwon et al., 2024b). In the stochastic NC-SC setting under bounded variance, the best-known first-order methods exhibit an ϵ−6\epsilon^{-6} dependence: the double-loop F3BSA method achieves 𝒪~​(κ¯y11​ϵ−6)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\bar{\kappa}_{y}^{11}\epsilon^{-6}) (Chen et al., 2025b), while the single-loop SGHA method achieves 𝒪⁡(κ¯y17​ϵ−6)\mathcal{O}(\bar{\kappa}_{y}^{17}\epsilon^{-6}) (Gu et al., 2026), where κ¯y\bar{\kappa}_{y} denotes the global condition number. Whether this ϵ−6\epsilon^{-6} dependence is unavoidable remains open.

More recently, Chen et al. (2025a) introduced a nested bilevel zero-chain construction, proving Ω⁡(κy2.5​ϵ−2)\Omega(\kappa_{y}^{2.5}\epsilon^{-2}) and Ω⁡(κy4.5​ϵ−4)\Omega(\kappa_{y}^{4.5}\epsilon^{-4}) lower bounds for zero-respecting algorithms on a constrained domain under the exact first-order oracle (ℱ​𝒪\mathcal{FO}) and the stochastic first-order oracle (𝒮​ℱ​𝒪\mathcal{SFO}), respectively, where κy\kappa_{y} denotes the lower-level condition number. Their construction uses a deterministic upper-level objective and a quadratic lower-level objective, with stochasticity entering through selected lower-level gradient responses. Although this yields a stronger dependence on κy\kappa_{y}, the stochastic lower bound scales only as ϵ−4\epsilon^{-4}, leaving an ϵ−2\epsilon^{-2} gap to the known ϵ−6\epsilon^{-6} upper bounds. This motivates the central question:

Does stochastic NC-SC bilevel optimization require Ω⁡(ϵ−6)\Omega(\epsilon^{-6}) standard 𝒮​ℱ​𝒪\mathcal{SFO} calls?

In this paper, we answer this question affirmatively. Under a standard stochastic first-order oracle, we prove that every randomized adaptive algorithm requires

Ω⁡(Δ​κy2ϵ2​max⁡{1,σ2​κy6ϵ4})\Omega\left(\frac{\Delta\kappa_{y}^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\max\left\{1,\frac{\sigma^{2}\kappa_{y}^{6}}{\epsilon^{4}}\right\}\right)

oracle calls to find an ϵ\epsilon-stationary point.

Our construction starts from the smooth nonconvex zero-chain of Carmon et al. (2020) and its stochastic extension in Arjevani et al. (2023). In these constructions, each oracle query can reveal at most one new relevant coordinate. We use a smooth indicator to distinguish the coordinates already revealed by previous oracle responses from the incoming coordinate, and randomize only the part of the objective associated with the incoming coordinate. This part appears in the stochastic lower-level oracle only when a fresh Bernoulli sample is successful.

To keep the bilevel problem unchanged, we place the incoming-coordinate term in a two-dimensional strongly convex quadratic block and add a compensation term. The lower-level minimizer remains explicit, and the resulting upper-level objective Φ\Phi coincides with the original zero-chain objective. The incoming-coordinate term enters the stochastic lower-level gradient with a coefficient of order κy−1\kappa_{y}^{-1}, while the relevant off-diagonal entry of the inverse lower Hessian has order κy\kappa_{y}. These two factors cancel in the hypergradient. Thus the stochastic lower-level gradient has smaller variance, while the corresponding component of ∇Φ\nabla\Phi has the same order as in the original zero-chain construction.

Finally, following the random-rotation arguments of Carmon et al. (2020) and Arjevani et al. (2023), the construction also applies to adaptive randomized first-order algorithms. The choice of the chain parameters gives T=Θ⁡(Δ​κy2​ϵ−2)T=\Theta\!\left(\Delta\kappa_{y}^{2}\epsilon^{-2}\right) coordinates, while the variance constraint permits a progress probability pp satisfying p−1=Θ⁡(max⁡{1,σ2​κy6​ϵ−4})p^{-1}=\Theta\!\left(\max\left\{1,\sigma^{2}\kappa_{y}^{6}\epsilon^{-4}\right\}\right). Since each successful Bernoulli sample increases the coordinate progress by at most one, the required number of oracle calls is of order T/pT/p. This gives Ω⁡(Δ​κy2​ϵ−2​max⁡{1,σ2​κy6​ϵ−4})\Omega\!\left(\Delta\kappa_{y}^{2}\epsilon^{-2}\max\left\{1,\sigma^{2}\kappa_{y}^{6}\epsilon^{-4}\right\}\right), which reduces to Ω⁡(Δ​σ2​κy8​ϵ−6)\Omega(\Delta\sigma^{2}\kappa_{y}^{8}\epsilon^{-6}) in the noise-dominated regime.

2 Related Work

Bilevel optimization.

Bilevel optimization has its roots in hierarchical decision making and Stackelberg games (von Stackelberg, 1934), and was introduced as a mathematical-programming model by Bracken and McGill (1973); see Colson et al. (2007) for an early survey. A classical approach to hypergradient computation is approximate implicit differentiation (AID). After approximately solving the lower-level problem, AID applies the implicit-function theorem and approximately solves a linear system involving ∇y​y2​g\nabla_{yy}^{2}g, typically using conjugate gradients or a truncated Neumann series (Domke, 2012; Pedregosa, 2016; Ghadimi and Wang, 2018; Grazzi et al., 2020). Iterative differentiation (ITD), by contrast, unrolls a finite number of lower-level iterations and differentiates through the resulting computational graph in either forward or reverse mode (Maclaurin et al., 2015; Franceschi et al., 2017; Shaban et al., 2019). Nonasymptotic analyses of AID and ITD for the NC-SC setting were developed by Ji et al. (2021), with subsequent extensions to stochastic and variance-reduced settings (Arbel and Mairal, 2021; Dagréou et al., 2022; Hong et al., 2023). Among these methods, stocBio (Ji et al., 2021) achieves the best-known HVP complexity of 𝒪~​(κ¯y6​ϵ−4)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\bar{\kappa}_{y}^{6}\epsilon^{-4}) under the stochastic NC-SC bilevel setting. Although these approaches avoid explicitly forming or inverting a Hessian, they usually require Hessian-vector products (HVP), which dominate the computational cost.

Several first-order methods have been developed for bilevel optimization, using only gradients of the upper- and lower-level objectives. Early approaches include value-function and penalty-based methods such as BOME and penalty-based bilevel gradient descent (Liu et al., 2022; Shen and Chen, 2023), followed by related penalty and sequential reformulations (Lu and Mei, 2024; Kwon et al., 2024b). The F2SA method (Kwon et al., 2023), based on approximately minimizing a penalized surrogate, achieves 𝒪~​(κ¯y7​ϵ−3)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\bar{\kappa}_{y}^{7}\epsilon^{-3}) deterministic complexity and 𝒪~​(poly⁡(κ¯y)​ϵ−7)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\operatorname{poly}(\bar{\kappa}_{y})\epsilon^{-7}) stochastic complexity, where κ¯y\bar{\kappa}_{y} denotes the global condition number. The F2BA/F2BSA framework of Chen et al. (2025b) improves these rates. In the deterministic NC-SC setting, F2BA achieves 𝒪~​(κ¯y4​ϵ−2)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\bar{\kappa}_{y}^{4}\epsilon^{-2}), and further improved to 𝒪~​(κ¯y7/2​ϵ−2)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\bar{\kappa}_{y}^{7/2}\epsilon^{-2}) by F2BA+ (Chen et al., 2025a). In the stochastic NC-SC setting, F2BSA achieves 𝒪~​(κ¯y12​ϵ−6)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\bar{\kappa}_{y}^{12}\epsilon^{-6}), and further improved to 𝒪~​(κ¯y11​ϵ−6)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\bar{\kappa}_{y}^{11}\epsilon^{-6}) by F3BSA (Chen et al., 2025b). Thus, the best-known fully first-order methods achieve only an ϵ−6\epsilon^{-6} dependence under standard stochastic first-order information, in contrast to the ϵ−4\epsilon^{-4} dependence attainable by HVP-based or variance-reduced methods under stronger smoothness assumptions (Ji et al., 2021; Arbel and Mairal, 2021).

Lower bounds and zero-chain constructions.

The modern lower-bound theory for first-order optimization originates from chain-structured quadratic instances used in convex optimization (Nemirovskij and Yudin, 1983; Nesterov, 2013). The essential feature of these instances is that first-order information can reveal new coordinates only sequentially. Carmon et al. (2020); Carmon et al. (2021) formalized this mechanism through zero-chains and developed robust zero-chain constructions for smooth nonconvex optimization. Their results include the classical Ω⁡(ϵ−2)\Omega(\epsilon^{-2}) lower bound for smooth nonconvex optimization under the first-order oracle, as well as the Ω(ϵ−12/7)\Omega(\epsilon^{-12/7}) and Ω(ϵ−8/5)\Omega(\epsilon^{-8/5}) lower bounds under second-order and arbitrarily high-order smoothness, respectively. In stochastic optimization, Arjevani et al. (2023) introduced probability-pp zero-chains together with random rotations and soft projections, establishing the tight Ω⁡(ϵ−4)\Omega(\epsilon^{-4}) lower bound under bounded variance and the Ω⁡(ϵ−3)\Omega(\epsilon^{-3}) lower bound under mean-squared smoothness. Random rotation is also the standard device for lifting coordinate-based zero-chain arguments beyond a fixed coordinate system (Carmon et al., 2020; Arjevani et al., 2023).

Lower bounds for general bilevel optimization are more recent. Liang and others (2023) established lower bounds for convex-strongly-convex and strongly-convex-strongly-convex bilevel problems under second-order oracle access. In finite-sum bilevel empirical-risk minimization, Dagréou et al. (2024) derived a matching finite-sum lower bound, while Chen et al. (2024) studied hardness phenomena that arise when the lower-level problem is not strongly convex.

For stochastic NC-SC bilevel optimization, Kwon et al. (2024a) established an Ω⁡(ϵ−6)\Omega(\epsilon^{-6}) lower bound under bounded variance and an Ω⁡(ϵ−4)\Omega(\epsilon^{-4}) lower bound under an additional stochastic-smoothness assumption. Their oracle is 𝒚∗\bm{y}^{*}-aware, supplying an O⁡(ϵ)O(\epsilon)-accurate approximation of 𝒚∗​(𝒙)\bm{y}^{*}(\bm{x}), while requiring the stochastic gradients to be unbiased only locally around 𝒚∗​(𝒙)\bm{y}^{*}(\bm{x}). Consequently, these lower bounds do not directly characterize the standard globally unbiased stochastic first-order oracle considered in this paper. More recently, Chen et al. (2025a) developed strengthened NC-SC bilevel lower bounds under standard first-order oracle models. In particular, they established Ω⁡(κy2.5​ϵ−2)\Omega(\kappa_{y}^{2.5}\epsilon^{-2}) and Ω⁡(κy4.5​ϵ−4)\Omega(\kappa_{y}^{4.5}\epsilon^{-4}) lower bounds for zero-respecting first-order algorithms on a constrained domain under deterministic and stochastic settings, respectively. As a special case of NC-SC bilevel optimization, NC-SC minimax optimization admits the lower bound Ω⁡(κy​ϵ−2+κy1/3​σ2​ϵ−4)\Omega\!\left(\sqrt{\kappa_{y}}\epsilon^{-2}+\kappa_{y}^{1/3}\sigma^{2}\epsilon^{-4}\right) (Li et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).

Our new lower bound closes the gap between the best-known ϵ−6\epsilon^{-6} first-order upper bound and the previous corresponding ϵ−4\epsilon^{-4} lower bound for stochastic NC-SC bilevel optimization. It shows that, under a stochastic first-order oracle, smooth NC-SC bilevel optimization can be strictly harder in its dependence on ϵ\epsilon than NC-SC minimax optimization, smooth nonconvex minimization, and bilevel optimization with access to Hessian-vector products.

3 Problem Setup

In this section, we introduce the bilevel function class considered in this paper, the algorithm class to which our lower bound applies, and the complexity measurement of the algorithms.

3.1 Function Class

To study the standard smooth nonconvex-strongly-convex (NC-SC) bilevel problem formulated in (1), we introduce the following class of functions.

Definition 3.1 (NC-SC bilevel function class).

Fix Lf,Lg,ρ,Cf,μg,Δ>0L_{f},L_{g},\rho,C_{f},\mu_{g},\Delta>0. We write ℱ⁡(Lf,Lg,ρ,Cf,μg,Δ)\mathcal{F}(L_{f},L_{g},\rho,C_{f},\mu_{g},\Delta) for the class of pairs f,g:ℝdx×ℝdy→ℝf,g:\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}\to\mathbb{R} satisfying the following conditions.

  1. 1.

    ∇f\nabla f and ∇g\nabla g are globally LfL_{f}– and LgL_{g}–Lipschitz, respectively.

  2. 2.

    g⁡(𝒙,⋅)g(\bm{x},\cdot) is μg\mu_{g}–strongly convex for every 𝒙\bm{x}.

  3. 3.

    The full Hessian ∇2g\nabla^{2}g is globally ρ\rho–Lipschitz.

  4. 4.

    The lower partial gradient of the upper-level objective is globally bounded, namely sup𝒙,𝒚‖∇yf​(𝒙,𝒚)‖≤Cf\sup_{\bm{x},\bm{y}}\left\lVert\nabla_{y}f(\bm{x},\bm{y})\right\rVert\leq C_{f}.

  5. 5.

    The hyper-objective Φ⁡(𝒙)\Phi(\bm{x}) is lower bounded and satisfies Φ⁡(𝟎)−inf𝒙Φ⁡(𝒙)≤Δ\Phi(\bm{0})-\inf_{\bm{x}}\Phi(\bm{x})\leq\Delta.

For the proof, we use two notions of condition numbers. The intrinsic condition number is determined by the actual lower-level Hessian, whereas the global condition number is defined by the parameters specifying the function class.

Definition 3.2 (Condition numbers).

For a pair (f,g)(f,g) in Definition 3.1, define the intrinsic lower-level curvature modulus and lower-level smoothness modulus by

μgact≔inf𝒙,𝒚λmin​(∇y​y2g​(𝒙,𝒚)),Ly≔sup𝒙,𝒚‖∇y​y2g​(𝒙,𝒚)‖op.\mu_{g}^{\rm act}\coloneqq\inf_{\bm{x},\bm{y}}\lambda_{\min}\!\left(\nabla^{2}_{yy}g(\bm{x},\bm{y})\right),\qquad L_{y}\coloneqq\sup_{\bm{x},\bm{y}}\left\lVert\nabla^{2}_{yy}g(\bm{x},\bm{y})\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}.

Define the aggregate Lipschitz constant by L¯≔max⁡{Cf,Lf,Lg,ρ}\bar{L}\coloneqq\max\left\{C_{f},L_{f},L_{g},\rho\right\}. The intrinsic lower-level and global condition numbers are, respectively,

κy≔Lyμgact,κ¯y≔L¯μg.\kappa_{y}\coloneqq\frac{L_{y}}{\mu_{g}^{\rm act}},\qquad\bar{\kappa}_{y}\coloneqq\frac{\bar{L}}{\mu_{g}}.

One always has κy≤κ¯y\kappa_{y}\leq\bar{\kappa}_{y}. For the hard instances constructed below, the intrinsic lower-level smoothness satisfies Ly=Θ⁡(1)L_{y}=\Theta(1) and the intrinsic curvature modulus satisfies μgact=Θ⁡(κ−1)\mu_{g}^{\rm act}=\Theta(\kappa^{-1}). Consequently, the intrinsic condition number satisfies κy=Θ⁡(κ)\kappa_{y}=\Theta(\kappa). Our lower bound is stated in terms of this intrinsic condition number.

3.2 Algorithm Class and Oracle Model

We consider randomized adaptive algorithms under the stochastic first-order oracle (𝒮​ℱ​𝒪\mathcal{SFO}). At each iteration, the next query may be any measurable function of the algorithm’s internal randomness and the previous query-response history. Let

𝖶≔ℝdx×ℝdy\mathsf{W}\coloneqq\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}

be the query space, and let

𝖸≔ℝdx+dy×ℝdx+dy\mathsf{Y}\coloneqq\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}+d_{y}}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}+d_{y}}

be the joint oracle-response space. For any t≥0t\geq 0, define the space of length-tt transcripts by

𝖳t≔(𝖶×𝖸)t,𝖳0≔{∅}.\mathsf{T}_{t}\coloneqq(\mathsf{W}\times\mathsf{Y})^{t},\qquad\mathsf{T}_{0}\coloneqq\{\varnothing\}.
Definition 3.3 (Randomized adaptive algorithm).

Fix an oracle-call budget N∈ℕ0N\in\mathbb{N}_{0}. A randomized adaptive algorithm 𝖠\mathsf{A} consists of a random seed ωalg\omega_{\rm alg} taking values in a standard Borel probability space, a sequence of Borel query maps

Queryt𝖠:Ωalg×𝖳t−1⟶𝖶,1≤t≤N,\operatorname{Query}_{t}^{\mathsf{A}}:\Omega_{\rm alg}\times\mathsf{T}_{t-1}\longrightarrow\mathsf{W},\qquad 1\leq t\leq N,

and a Borel output map

OutputN𝖠:Ωalg×𝖳N⟶ℝdx.\operatorname{Output}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}}:\Omega_{\rm alg}\times\mathsf{T}_{N}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}.

Given an oracle, the interaction is defined recursively. Starting from the empty transcript 𝒯0=∅\mathcal{T}_{0}=\varnothing, at call tt the algorithm selects

𝒘t=(𝒙t,𝒚t)=Queryt𝖠⁡(ωalg,𝒯t−1),\bm{w}_{t}=(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{y}_{t})=\operatorname{Query}_{t}^{\mathsf{A}}(\omega_{\rm alg},\mathcal{T}_{t-1}),

receives an oracle response 𝒀t∈𝖸\bm{Y}_{t}\in\mathsf{Y}, and forms

𝒯t=(𝒯t−1,𝒘t,𝒀t)∈𝖳t.\mathcal{T}_{t}=\bigl(\mathcal{T}_{t-1},\bm{w}_{t},\bm{Y}_{t}\bigr)\in\mathsf{T}_{t}.

After NN calls, the algorithm returns

𝒙^N𝖠=OutputN𝖠⁡(ωalg,𝒯N).\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}}=\operatorname{Output}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}}(\omega_{\rm alg},\mathcal{T}_{N}).

The pre-query information before call tt is the sigma-field

ℱt−1≔σ⁡(ωalg,𝒯t−1).\mathscr{F}_{t-1}\coloneqq\sigma\bigl(\omega_{\rm alg},\mathcal{T}_{t-1}\bigr).

Thus 𝒘t\bm{w}_{t} is ℱt−1\mathscr{F}_{t-1}-measurable. We denote by 𝒜N𝒮​ℱ​𝒪​(dx,dy)\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\mathcal{SFO}}(d_{x},d_{y}) the class of all such algorithms making at most NN stochastic first-order oracle calls. When the dimensions are clear, we simply write 𝒜N𝒮​ℱ​𝒪\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\mathcal{SFO}}.

An algorithm that stops before call NN is included in 𝒜N𝒮​ℱ​𝒪\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\mathcal{SFO}} by allowing its output map to ignore all subsequent oracle responses. No zero-respecting, linear-span, or other structural restriction is imposed on the query maps.

We next introduce the stochastic first-order oracle.

Definition 3.4 (Stochastic first-order oracle (𝒮​ℱ​𝒪\mathcal{SFO})).

At a query (𝒙t,𝒚t)(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{y}_{t}), a joint stochastic first-order oracle returns

𝒀t=𝕆𝒮​ℱ​𝒪​(𝒙t,𝒚t,ζt,ξt)=(𝑮f​(𝒙t,𝒚t,ζt),𝑮g​(𝒙t,𝒚t,ξt)).\bm{Y}_{t}=\mathbb{O}^{\mathcal{SFO}}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{y}_{t};\zeta_{t},\xi_{t})=\bigl(\bm{G}_{f}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{y}_{t};\zeta_{t}),\bm{G}_{g}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{y}_{t};\xi_{t})\bigr).

The fresh sample pair (ζt,ξt)(\zeta_{t},\xi_{t}) is independent of the pre-query sigma-field ℱt−1\mathscr{F}_{t-1}. At every possibly random query generated by an algorithm in 𝒜N𝒮​ℱ​𝒪\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\mathcal{SFO}}, the oracle satisfies

𝔼⁡[𝑮f​(𝒙t,𝒚t,ζt)|ℱt−1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\bm{G}_{f}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{y}_{t};\zeta_{t})\,\middle|\,\mathscr{F}_{t-1}\right] =∇f​(𝒙t,𝒚t),\displaystyle=\nabla f(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{y}_{t}), 𝔼⁡[‖𝑮f​(𝒙t,𝒚t,ζt)−∇f​(𝒙t,𝒚t)‖2|ℱt−1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\lVert\bm{G}_{f}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{y}_{t};\zeta_{t})-\nabla f(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{y}_{t})\right\rVert^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathscr{F}_{t-1}\right] ≤σ2,\displaystyle\leq\sigma^{2},
𝔼⁡[𝑮g​(𝒙t,𝒚t,ξt)|ℱt−1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\bm{G}_{g}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{y}_{t};\xi_{t})\,\middle|\,\mathscr{F}_{t-1}\right] =∇g​(𝒙t,𝒚t),\displaystyle=\nabla g(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{y}_{t}), 𝔼⁡[‖𝑮g​(𝒙t,𝒚t,ξt)−∇g​(𝒙t,𝒚t)‖2|ℱt−1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\lVert\bm{G}_{g}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{y}_{t};\xi_{t})-\nabla g(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{y}_{t})\right\rVert^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathscr{F}_{t-1}\right] ≤σ2.\displaystyle\leq\sigma^{2}.

We write 𝕆σ𝒮​ℱ​𝒪​(f,g)\mathbb{O}_{\sigma}^{\mathcal{SFO}}(f,g) for the collection of all such oracles for the function pair (f,g)(f,g).

3.3 Worst-Case Oracle Complexity

Since the hyper-objective Φ\Phi in (1) is nonconvex, global optimization may require exponentially many oracle calls in the worst case (Nemirovskij and Yudin, 1983). We therefore use the standard first-order stationarity criterion from smooth nonconvex optimization (Carmon et al., 2020; Carmon et al., 2021; Arjevani et al., 2023).

Definition 3.5 (ϵ\epsilon-stationarity).

A possibly random point 𝒙^∈ℝdx\widehat{\bm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}} is called an ϵ\epsilon-stationary output of Φ\Phi if

𝔼​‖∇Φ​(𝒙^)‖≤ϵ,\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\nabla\Phi(\widehat{\bm{x}})\right\rVert\leq\epsilon, (2)

where the expectation is taken over all randomness of the algorithm and the stochastic oracle.

For a function class ℱ\mathcal{F} and an associated family of admissible stochastic oracles 𝕆σ𝒮​ℱ​𝒪\mathbb{O}_{\sigma}^{\mathcal{SFO}}, define the worst-case risk after NN oracle calls by

ℜN𝒮​ℱ​𝒪​(𝒜𝒮​ℱ​𝒪,ℱ,𝕆σ𝒮​ℱ​𝒪)≔inf𝖠∈𝒜N𝒮​ℱ​𝒪sup(f,g)∈ℱsup𝕆∈𝕆σ𝒮​ℱ​𝒪​(f,g)𝔼𝖠,𝕆​‖∇Φ​(𝒙^N𝖠)‖.\displaystyle\mathfrak{R}_{N}^{\mathcal{SFO}}\bigl(\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{SFO}},\mathcal{F},\mathbb{O}_{\sigma}^{\mathcal{SFO}}\bigr)\coloneqq\inf_{\mathsf{A}\in\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\mathcal{SFO}}}\sup_{(f,g)\in\mathcal{F}}\sup_{\mathbb{O}\in\mathbb{O}_{\sigma}^{\mathcal{SFO}}(f,g)}\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{A},\mathbb{O}}\left\lVert\nabla\Phi\bigl(\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}}\bigr)\right\rVert. (3)

Here 𝒙^N𝖠\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}} denotes the output of 𝖠\mathsf{A} after at most NN oracle calls.

Definition 3.6 (Worst-case oracle complexity).

The worst-case 𝒮​ℱ​𝒪\mathcal{SFO} complexity for finding an ϵ\epsilon-stationary point is

Complϵ𝒮​ℱ​𝒪​(𝒜𝒮​ℱ​𝒪,ℱ,𝕆σ𝒮​ℱ​𝒪)≔inf{N∈ℕ0:ℜN𝒮​ℱ​𝒪​(𝒜𝒮​ℱ​𝒪,ℱ,𝕆σ𝒮​ℱ​𝒪)≤ϵ}.\operatorname{Compl}_{\epsilon}^{\mathcal{SFO}}(\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{SFO}},\mathcal{F},\mathbb{O}_{\sigma}^{\mathcal{SFO}})\coloneqq\inf\left\{N\in\mathbb{N}_{0}:\mathfrak{R}_{N}^{\mathcal{SFO}}(\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{SFO}},\mathcal{F},\mathbb{O}_{\sigma}^{\mathcal{SFO}})\leq\epsilon\right\}. (4)

Definition 3.6 follows the uniform minimax convention: a single algorithm is chosen before the worst-case objective function and stochastic oracle are selected. This quantifier order is consistent with our lower-bound statement, which states that for every randomized adaptive algorithm there exist an instance and an admissible oracle on which the algorithm requires the claimed number of oracle calls.

4 Lower Bound for Stochastic NC-SC Bilevel Optimization

In this section, we first construct and analyze the hard instance for a fixed orthonormal frame, including the parameter choice. We then randomize the frame to obtain the progress bound for randomized adaptive algorithms. The proofs are given in the appendices.

4.1 Main Result

Theorem 4.1.

There are universal positive constants cLB,cϵ,L¯f,L¯g,ρ¯c_{\rm LB},c_{\epsilon},\bar{L}_{f},\bar{L}_{g},\bar{\rho} with the following property. Fix any Δ>0\Delta>0. There is a finite constant C¯f​(Δ)>0\bar{C}_{f}(\Delta)>0, depending only on Δ\Delta, such that, for every κ≥2\kappa\geq 2, σ≥0\sigma\geq 0, and ϵ\epsilon satisfying

0<ϵ≤cϵ​min⁡{1,Δ},0<\epsilon\leq c_{\epsilon}\min\{1,\sqrt{\Delta}\}, (5)

and every N∈ℕ0N\in\mathbb{N}_{0} satisfying

N≤cLB​Δ​κ2ϵ2​max⁡{1,σ2​κ6ϵ4},N\leq c_{\rm LB}\frac{\Delta\kappa^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\max\left\{1,\frac{\sigma^{2}\kappa^{6}}{\epsilon^{4}}\right\}, (6)

there exists a finite dimension dd such that, for every 𝖠∈𝒜N𝒮​ℱ​𝒪​(d,d+2)\mathsf{A}\in\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\mathcal{SFO}}(d,d+2), there exist a pair (f,g)∈ℱ⁡(L¯f,L¯g,ρ¯,C¯f​(Δ),(2​κ)−1,Δ)(f,g)\in\mathcal{F}(\bar{L}_{f},\bar{L}_{g},\bar{\rho},\bar{C}_{f}(\Delta),(2\kappa)^{-1},\Delta) and an oracle 𝕆∈𝕆σ𝒮​ℱ​𝒪​(f,g)\mathbb{O}\in\mathbb{O}_{\sigma}^{\mathcal{SFO}}(f,g) such that the output 𝐱^N𝖠\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}} obeys

𝔼𝖠,𝕆​‖∇Φ​(𝒙^N𝖠)‖>32​ϵ,𝔼𝖠,𝕆​‖∇Φ​(𝒙^N𝖠)‖2>94​ϵ2.\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{A},\mathbb{O}}\left\lVert\nabla\Phi(\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}})\right\rVert>\frac{3}{2}\epsilon,\qquad\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{A},\mathbb{O}}\left\lVert\nabla\Phi(\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}})\right\rVert^{2}>\frac{9}{4}\epsilon^{2}. (7)

In particular,

ℜN𝒮​ℱ​𝒪​(𝒜𝒮​ℱ​𝒪,ℱ⁡(L¯f,L¯g,ρ¯,C¯f​(Δ),(2​κ)−1,Δ),𝕆σ𝒮​ℱ​𝒪)≥32​ϵ>ϵ.\mathfrak{R}_{N}^{\mathcal{SFO}}\bigl(\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{SFO}},\mathcal{F}(\bar{L}_{f},\bar{L}_{g},\bar{\rho},\bar{C}_{f}(\Delta),(2\kappa)^{-1},\Delta),\mathbb{O}_{\sigma}^{\mathcal{SFO}}\bigr)\geq\frac{3}{2}\epsilon>\epsilon.

Finally, as the intrinsic condition number of the constructed lower problem satisfies κ≤κy≤14​κ\kappa\leq\kappa_{y}\leq 14\kappa, the complexity bound can equivalently be expressed as

Ω⁡(Δ​κy2ϵ2​max⁡{1,σ2​κy6ϵ4}).\Omega\!\left(\frac{\Delta\kappa_{y}^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\max\left\{1,\frac{\sigma^{2}\kappa_{y}^{6}}{\epsilon^{4}}\right\}\right). (8)

By Theorem 4.1, the noise-dominated term is Ω⁡(Δ​σ2​κy8​ϵ−6)\Omega\!\left(\Delta\sigma^{2}\kappa_{y}^{8}\epsilon^{-6}\right). To our knowledge, this is the first ϵ−6\epsilon^{-6} complexity lower bound for smooth stochastic NC-SC bilevel optimization under the standard stochastic first-order oracle, showing that the ϵ\epsilon-dependence of the existing upper bounds is optimal (Chen et al., 2025b; Gu et al., 2026). When σ=0\sigma=0, the same construction yields a deterministic lower bound Ω⁡(Δ​κy2​ϵ−2)\Omega\!\left(\Delta\kappa_{y}^{2}\epsilon^{-2}\right) for randomized algorithms. This is slightly weaker in its dependence on κy\kappa_{y} than the deterministic lower bound of Chen et al. (2025a), which establishes the bound Ω⁡(Δ​κy2.5​ϵ−2)\Omega\!\left(\Delta\kappa_{y}^{2.5}\epsilon^{-2}\right).

We emphasize that the theorem is high-dimensional. Once the parameters and the oracle-call budget NN are fixed, the ambient dimension dd is chosen sufficiently large, uniformly over all algorithms in 𝒜N𝒮​ℱ​𝒪​(d,d+2)\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\mathcal{SFO}}(d,d+2). A sufficient choice of dd is given in (84). Thus, the theorem does not assert an ϵ−6\epsilon^{-6} lower bound in any fixed finite dimension.

The proof has an analytic part and a probabilistic part. The analytic part shows that the hypergradient is large whenever the coordinate progress is below TT. The probabilistic part shows that, below the stated call budget, the coordinate progress remains below TT with constant probability. The hard instance is first defined relative to a fixed orthonormal frame. η\eta sets the scale of the rescaled zero-chain: each chain coordinate contributes O⁡(η2)O(\eta^{2}) to the initial gap, while the corresponding gradient scale is O⁡(η)O(\eta). TT is the number of chain coordinates, and pp is the success probability of the fresh Bernoulli variable that permits dependence on the next relevant coordinate. The random rotation hides the fixed frame and is used only in the probabilistic progress argument.

We choose T=Θ⁡(Δ/η2)T=\Theta(\Delta/\eta^{2}), which uses the initial-gap budget up to numerical constants. The stochastic lower-level oracle randomizes a compensated perturbation inside a two-dimensional strongly convex quadratic block, with gradient norm O⁡(η2/κ)O(\eta^{2}/\kappa). After Bernoulli importance weighting, its contribution to the oracle variance is bounded by O⁡(η4/(p​κ2))O(\eta^{4}/(p\kappa^{2})). We therefore choose pp as p−1=Θ⁡(max⁡{1,σ2​κ2​η−4})p^{-1}=\Theta\!\left(\max\{1,\sigma^{2}\kappa^{2}\eta^{-4}\}\right), and further choose η=Θ⁡(ϵ/κ)\eta=\Theta(\epsilon/\kappa) so that the hypergradient at any point with coordinate progress below TT exceeds ϵ\epsilon. Combining these three relations with the T/pT/p query bound for the probability-pp zero-chain gives the κ8​ϵ−6\kappa^{8}\epsilon^{-6} term in the noise-dominated regime. The random rotation affects the dimension required for the progress argument but does not change this parameter scaling.

4.2 Hard Instance Construction

In the hard bilevel instance constructed below, the lower variable is denoted by 𝒚=(𝒛,𝒗)∈ℝd×ℝ2\bm{y}=(\bm{z},\bm{v})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{2}. The 𝒛\bm{z}-block yields 𝒛∗​(𝒙)=κ​𝒙\bm{z}^{*}(\bm{x})=\kappa\bm{x}. The two-dimensional 𝒗\bm{v}-block scales the gradient contribution of the compensated term by Θ⁡(κ−1)\Theta(\kappa^{-1}), while preserving the corresponding term in the hyper-objective after the lower problem is minimized.

Throughout this section, every symbol of the form C∙C_{\bullet} denotes a fixed numerical constant independent of T,d,𝑼,η,κ,Δ,σT,d,\bm{U},\eta,\kappa,\Delta,\sigma, and ϵ\epsilon. The class bound C¯f​(Δ)\bar{C}_{f}(\Delta) is allowed to depend on Δ\Delta, as stated in Lemma 4.7.

Following the zero-chain construction of Carmon et al. (2020), define

FT​(𝒂)=∑i=1TQ⁡(ai−1,ai).F_{T}(\bm{a})=\sum_{i=1}^{T}Q(a_{i-1},a_{i}). (11)

The function Hη,TH_{\eta,T} has a sequential dependence structure. Its iith summand depends on coordinates i−1i-1 and ii, and for i≥2i\geq 2 this summand and all of its derivatives vanish when |zi−1|≤η/2\lvert z_{i-1}\rvert\leq\eta/2. The quantity progη⁡(𝒛)\operatorname{prog}_{\eta}(\bm{z}) is the largest index whose coordinate has magnitude greater than η\eta. If j=progη⁡(𝒛)+1≤Tj=\operatorname{prog}_{\eta}(\bm{z})+1\leq T, then Lemma 4.2 gives |∂jHη,T​(𝒛)|≥η\lvert\partial_{j}H_{\eta,T}(\bm{z})\rvert\geq\eta. (2023); see, e.g., the derivative and zero-chain bounds around Lemmas 2–3 and 6–7 of Arjevani et al. (2023). We state the scaled form needed here and omit the proof.

There are fixed numerical constants CΔ,Cch,2,Cch,3>0C_{\Delta},C_{{\rm ch},2},C_{{\rm ch},3}>0 such that, for all T≥1T\geq 1, 0<η≤10<\eta\leq 1, and 𝐳∈ℝT\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{T},

and

By (12), for every r≥0r\geq 0,

Dr​Hη,T​(𝒛)=η2−r​Dr​FT​(𝒛/η).D^{r}H_{\eta,T}(\bm{z})=\eta^{2-r}D^{r}F_{T}(\bm{z}/\eta). (17)

4.2.2 Smooth Decomposition of the Zero-chain

For the stochastic construction, we use soft indicators of the tail coordinates zi,…,zTz_{i},\ldots,z_{T} to isolate the incoming-coordinate summand for randomization. This decomposition adapts the smooth probability-pp zero-chain construction of Arjevani et al. (2023, Sections 3.3 and 5.1) by rescaling it with parameter η\eta. Let

χ+​(s)={0,s≤0,e−1/s,s>0,\chi_{+}(s)=\begin{cases}0,&s\leq 0,\\ e^{-1/s},&s>0,\end{cases}

and, for a<ba<b, define the flat transition

γa,b​(t)=χ+​(t−a)χ+​(t−a)+χ+​(b−t).\gamma_{a,b}(t)=\frac{\chi_{+}(t-a)}{\chi_{+}(t-a)+\chi_{+}(b-t)}. (18)

γa,b​(t)\gamma_{a,b}(t) is C∞C^{\infty}, equals zero on (−∞,a](-\infty,a], equals one on [b,∞)[b,\infty), and satisfies γa,b(r)​(a)=γa,b(r)​(b)=0\gamma_{a,b}^{(r)}(a)=\gamma_{a,b}^{(r)}(b)=0 for every integer r≥1r\geq 1. Define

Γ​(t)=γ1/4,1/2​(t),\displaystyle\Gamma(t)=\gamma_{1/4,1/2}(t), υ⁡(t)=Γ⁡(|t|),\displaystyle\quad\upsilon(t)=\Gamma\!\left(\left\lvert t\right\rvert\right), (19)
𝑽iη​(𝒛)=(υ⁡(zi/η),…,υ⁡(zT/η)),\displaystyle\bm{V}_{i}^{\eta}(\bm{z})=\bigl(\upsilon(z_{i}/\eta),\ldots,\upsilon(z_{T}/\eta)\bigr), hiη​(𝒛)=Γ⁡(1−‖𝑽iη​(𝒛)‖).\displaystyle\quad h_{i}^{\eta}(\bm{z})=\Gamma\!\left(1-\left\lVert\bm{V}_{i}^{\eta}(\bm{z})\right\rVert\right). (20)

Indeed, if 𝒙=𝒛/η\bm{x}=\bm{z}/\eta, then hiη​(𝒛)h_{i}^{\eta}(\bm{z}) has the same tail-norm form as the smooth progress indicator Θi​(𝒙)\Theta_{i}(\bm{x}) in Arjevani et al. (2023, Eq. (19)), up to the particular choice of the one-dimensional transition function. The thresholds η/4\eta/4 and η/2\eta/2 define a fixed transition region. A tail coordinate with magnitude greater than η/2\eta/2 makes every corresponding soft indicator vanish locally, while the flatness of the chain summands eliminates terms lying more than one coordinate beyond the current progress index.

Finally, define

bη,T​(𝒛)=η2​∑i=1Thiη​(𝒛)​ℒiη​(𝒛),Aη,T​(𝒛)=Hη,T​(𝒛)−bη,T​(𝒛).b_{\eta,T}(\bm{z})=\eta^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{T}h_{i}^{\eta}(\bm{z})\mathcal{L}_{i}^{\eta}(\bm{z}),\qquad A_{\eta,T}(\bm{z})=H_{\eta,T}(\bm{z})-b_{\eta,T}(\bm{z}). (21)

For ξ∼Ber⁡(p)\xi\sim\operatorname{Ber}(p), randomizing only bη,Tb_{\eta,T} in the decomposition Hη,T=Aη,T+bη,TH_{\eta,T}=A_{\eta,T}+b_{\eta,T} gives

Aη,T​(𝒛)+ξp​bη,T​(𝒛)=Hη,T​(𝒛)+(ξp−1)​bη,T​(𝒛).A_{\eta,T}(\bm{z})+\frac{\xi}{p}b_{\eta,T}(\bm{z})=H_{\eta,T}(\bm{z})+\left(\frac{\xi}{p}-1\right)b_{\eta,T}(\bm{z}).

This has the same importance-weighted form as the randomized zero-chain in Arjevani et al. (2023, Eq. (31)). In our bilevel construction, however, we do not randomize the chain function directly. Instead, Aη,TA_{\eta,T} enters the deterministic upper-level term, while bη,Tb_{\eta,T} is used to construct the compensated lower-level block, which is multiplied in its entirety by ξ/p\xi/p.

Although bη,Tb_{\eta,T} is written as a sum of TT terms, at any point at most one summand can have a nonzero derivative of order at most three. The next lemma gives this derivative bound together with the required coordinate-dependence identities. Its proof is given in Appendix A.

Aη,T​(𝒛)=Aη,T​(𝑷k​𝒛),\displaystyle A_{\eta,T}(\bm{z})=A_{\eta,T}(\bm{P}_{k}\bm{z}), bη,T​(𝒛)=bη,T​(𝑷k+1​𝒛),\displaystyle b_{\eta,T}(\bm{z})=b_{\eta,T}(\bm{P}_{k+1}\bm{z}), (23)

4.2.3 Bilevel Objectives and Stochastic Oracle

Define an even, compactly supported cutoff function

ω⁡(t)=1−γ1,2​(|t|),ω⁡(t)={1,|t|≤1,0,|t|≥2.\omega(t)=1-\gamma_{1,2}(\lvert t\rvert),\qquad\omega(t)=\begin{cases}1,&|t|\leq 1,\\ 0,&|t|\geq 2.\end{cases} (26)

It remains to relate the progress index to the number of successful Bernoulli samples. Let

SN=∑t=1Nξt.S_{N}=\sum_{t=1}^{N}\xi_{t}.

Freshness gives 𝔼​SN=N​p\mathbb{E}S_{N}=Np. Hence, whenever N≤T/(8​p)N\leq T/(8p), Markov’s inequality yields

ℙ⁡(SN≥T)≤𝔼​SNT=N​pT≤18.\mathbb{P}(S_{N}\geq T)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}S_{N}}{T}=\frac{Np}{T}\leq\frac{1}{8}. (70)

Under the dimension condition stated below, the random-rotation argument in Section 4.5 shows, with probability at least 7/87/8, that

progη/4⁡(𝑼⊤​ρR​(κ​𝒙^N𝖠))≤min⁡{T,SN}.\operatorname{prog}_{\eta/4}\!\left(\bm{U}^{\top}\rho_{R}(\kappa\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}})\right)\leq\min\{T,S_{N}\}. (71)

Together with (70), this implies that the rotated chain coordinates at the output have progress below TT with probability at least 3/43/4. Equation (67) then gives

𝔼⁡‖∇Φ𝑼κ​(𝒙^N𝖠)‖>34​(2​ϵ)=32​ϵ>ϵ.\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\nabla\Phi_{\bm{U}}^{\kappa}(\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}})\right\rVert>\frac{3}{4}(2\epsilon)=\frac{3}{2}\epsilon>\epsilon.

If the frame 𝑼\bm{U} were known to the algorithm, one query could have nonzero components in many chain directions, and (71) would not hold. We will therefore take 𝑼\bm{U} to be Haar-uniform and prove the progress bound with high probability. This step does not alter η\eta, TT, or pp.

4.5 Random Rotation for Adaptive Randomized Algorithms

We compare the geometric progress of the queries with the Bernoulli success count. For the point queried on call tt, define

kt≔progη/4⁡(𝑼⊤​ρR​(𝒛t)).k_{t}\coloneqq\operatorname{prog}_{\eta/4}\!\left(\bm{U}^{\top}\rho_{R}(\bm{z}_{t})\right). (72)

The number of successful Bernoulli draws and the corresponding upper bound on coordinate progress are

St≔∑s=1tξs,Lt≔min⁡{T,St},S0=L0=0.S_{t}\coloneqq\sum_{s=1}^{t}\xi_{s},\qquad L_{t}\coloneqq\min\{T,S_{t}\},\qquad S_{0}=L_{0}=0. (73)

The goal is to prove, with high probability, that kt≤Lt−1k_{t}\leq L_{t-1} before call tt. On this event, a response with ξt=0\xi_{t}=0 depends only on the first Lt−1L_{t-1} frame columns, whereas a response with ξt=1\xi_{t}=1 may depend on one additional frame column. This dependence on the initial frame columns is combined with the spherical-cap estimate in the coupled induction below.

4.5.1 Random-rotation Lemmas

If the frame were fixed and known, an adaptive algorithm could query a vector with nonzero components in all chain directions. We therefore choose

𝑼=(𝒖1,…,𝒖T)\bm{U}=(\bm{u}_{1},\ldots,\bm{u}_{T})

Haar-uniformly from the Stiefel manifold

St⁡(d,T)={𝑽∈ℝd×T:𝑽⊤​𝑽=𝑰T}.\operatorname{St}(d,T)=\left\{\bm{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times T}:\bm{V}^{\top}\bm{V}=\bm{I}_{T}\right\}.

The coordinates of an ambient vector 𝒓∈ℝd\bm{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} in the random frame are then

𝑼⊤​𝒓=(⟨𝒖1,𝒓⟩,…,⟨𝒖T,𝒓⟩).\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{r}=\bigl(\left\langle\bm{u}_{1},\bm{r}\right\rangle,\ldots,\left\langle\bm{u}_{T},\bm{r}\right\rangle\bigr).

The proof constructs a coupled transcript whose dependence on 𝑼\bm{U} is through a random number of initial frame columns. Conditional on the sigma-field defined below, the remaining columns have the Haar-completion law on the orthogonal complement of the span of the recorded frame columns. The spherical-cap bound therefore controls the inner product of a bounded adaptive query with each remaining column.

The number of recorded frame columns is random because it depends on the previous Bernoulli samples. A conditional Haar statement for a fixed number of initial columns therefore cannot be applied directly with a random index. The next lemma applies the corresponding conditional law separately on each event {J=ℓ}\{J=\ell\} and combines the resulting identities. This justifies the corresponding conditioning for the adaptive transcript. For a frame 𝑼\bm{U}, write 𝑼≤ℓ=(𝒖1,…,𝒖ℓ)\bm{U}_{\leq\ell}=(\bm{u}_{1},\ldots,\bm{u}_{\ell}). Its proof is given in Appendix C.1.

Lemma 4.10.

Let T≥1T\geq 1, d≥Td\geq T, let 𝐔\bm{U} be Haar-uniform on St⁡(d,T)\operatorname{St}(d,T), and let ZZ be an independent random element of a standard Borel space. Let J=J⁡(Z)∈{0,…,T}J=J(Z)\in\{0,\ldots,T\} be Borel measurable. For each deterministic ℓ\ell, let 𝖪ℓ​(𝐔≤ℓ,⋅)\mathsf{K}_{\ell}(\bm{U}_{\leq\ell},\cdot) denote the canonical Haar-completion kernel on the orthogonal complement of span⁡(𝐔≤ℓ)\operatorname{span}(\bm{U}_{\leq\ell}), with the evident point mass interpretation when ℓ=T\ell=T. Define ℋJ\mathscr{H}_{J} stratumwise by

E∈ℋJ⟺E∩{J=ℓ}∈σ(Z,𝑼≤ℓ)for every 0≤ℓ≤T.E\in\mathscr{H}_{J}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad E\cap\{J=\ell\}\in\sigma(Z,\bm{U}_{\leq\ell})\quad\text{for every }0\leq\ell\leq T.

Then, for every bounded Borel function φ⁡(Z,𝐔)\varphi(Z,\bm{U}),

𝔼[φ(Z,𝑼)∣ℋJ]=∑ℓ=0T𝟏{J=ℓ}∫φ(Z,(𝑼≤ℓ,𝑽))𝖪ℓ(𝑼≤ℓ,d𝑽)a.s.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\varphi(Z,\bm{U})\mid\mathscr{H}_{J}\right]=\sum_{\ell=0}^{T}\bm{1}_{\{J=\ell\}}\int\varphi\bigl(Z,(\bm{U}_{\leq\ell},\bm{V})\bigr)\,\mathsf{K}_{\ell}(\bm{U}_{\leq\ell},d\bm{V})\quad\text{a.s.}

Consequently, on {J=ℓ<T}\{J=\ell<T\}, each column 𝐮j\bm{u}_{j} with j>ℓj>\ell has, conditionally on ℋJ\mathscr{H}_{J}, the uniform spherical marginal in span⁡(𝐔≤ℓ)⟂\operatorname{span}(\bm{U}_{\leq\ell})^{\perp}.

The next lemma states the random-rotation argument for a probability-pp zero-chain. Given the first ℓ\ell frame directions, a response with ξt=0\xi_{t}=0 depends on no additional direction, whereas a response with ξt=1\xi_{t}=1 may depend on direction ℓ+1\ell+1. In sufficiently high dimension, spherical concentration then bounds the coordinate progress of the vector associated with an adaptive query by ℓ\ell with high probability. Its proof is given in Appendix C.2.

Lemma 4.11.

There is a numerical constant CH>0C_{\rm H}>0 with the following property. Fix η>0\eta>0 and R>ηR>\eta. Let T≥1T\geq 1, d≥Td\geq T, and let 𝐔=(𝐮1,…,𝐮T)\bm{U}=(\bm{u}_{1},\ldots,\bm{u}_{T}) be Haar-uniform on St⁡(d,T)\operatorname{St}(d,T). Consider an arbitrary randomized adaptive procedure with random seed ωalg\omega_{\rm alg} that makes NN calls. Let 𝒯t−1∈𝖳t−1\mathcal{T}_{t-1}\in\mathsf{T}_{t-1} denote its actual transcript before call tt, and define its pre-query information by

ℱt−1=σ⁡(ωalg,𝒯t−1).\mathscr{F}_{t-1}=\sigma\bigl(\omega_{\rm alg},\mathcal{T}_{t-1}\bigr).

Let 𝖣\mathsf{D} be a standard Borel space containing the public query data used by the oracle. Before call tt, the procedure chooses a query descriptor 𝐚t∈𝖣\bm{a}_{t}\in\mathsf{D} and an associated vector 𝐫t∈ℝd\bm{r}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, both measurable with respect to ℱt−1\mathscr{F}_{t-1}, such that

‖𝒓t‖≤Rη.\left\lVert\bm{r}_{t}\right\rVert\leq\frac{R}{\eta}. (74)

Let p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1], and let ξ1,…,ξN\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{N} be i.i.d. Ber⁡(p)\operatorname{Ber}(p) variables such that 𝐔\bm{U}, ωalg\omega_{\rm alg}, and (ξ1,…,ξN)(\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{N}) are mutually independent. At call tt, the oracle uses ξt\xi_{t}. In particular, ξt\xi_{t} is independent of the actual pre-query sigma-field ℱt−1\mathscr{F}_{t-1}. Let 𝐘t\bm{Y}_{t} denote the oracle response, taking values in a standard Borel response space 𝖸\mathsf{Y}. We impose the following response-dependence condition. For every t∈{1,…,N}t\in\{1,\ldots,N\}, integer ℓ∈{0,…,T}\ell\in\{0,\ldots,T\}, and bit b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}, there is a Borel map

Mt,ℓ(b):𝖳t−1×𝖣×ℝd×St⁡(d,ℓb)⟶𝖸,ℓb=min⁡{T,ℓ+b},M_{t,\ell}^{(b)}:\mathsf{T}_{t-1}\times\mathsf{D}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\operatorname{St}(d,\ell_{b})\longrightarrow\mathsf{Y},\qquad\ell_{b}=\min\{T,\ell+b\}, (75)

where 𝖳t−1\mathsf{T}_{t-1} is the transcript space before call tt, such that, on the event

{ξt=b,prog1/4(𝑼⊤𝒓t)≤ℓ},\left\{\xi_{t}=b,\quad\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}(\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{r}_{t})\leq\ell\right\}, (76)

the actual response satisfies

𝒀t=Mt,ℓ(b)​(𝒯t−1,𝒂t,𝒓t,𝒖1,…,𝒖ℓb).\bm{Y}_{t}=M_{t,\ell}^{(b)}\bigl(\mathcal{T}_{t-1},\bm{a}_{t},\bm{r}_{t},\bm{u}_{1},\ldots,\bm{u}_{\ell_{b}}\bigr). (77)

Thus a failed call has a representation using only the first ℓ\ell columns, while a successful call has a representation using only the first min⁡{T,ℓ+1}\min\{T,\ell+1\} columns. The requirement is the existence of the uniform Borel maps in (75); a pointwise statement that happens to mention no later column is not sufficient. After the NN calls, append an additional vector 𝐫N+1\bm{r}_{N+1} determined by the procedure’s output and satisfying ‖𝐫N+1‖≤Rη\left\lVert\bm{r}_{N+1}\right\rVert\leq\frac{R}{\eta}, but return no oracle response to this vector. Put n=N+1n=N+1. If δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) and

d≥T+CH​(Rη)2​n​log⁡(2​n2​Tδ),d\geq T+C_{\rm H}(\frac{R}{\eta})^{2}n\log\left(\frac{2n^{2}T}{\delta}\right), (78)

then, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, simultaneously,

prog1/4⁡(𝑼⊤​𝒓t)≤Lt−1,1≤t≤N,\displaystyle\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}(\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{r}_{t})\leq L_{t-1},\quad 1\leq t\leq N, (79)
prog1/4⁡(𝑼⊤​𝒓N+1)≤LN.\displaystyle\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}(\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{r}_{N+1})\leq L_{N}. (80)

The probability is joint over 𝐔\bm{U}, the procedure’s private randomness, and the fresh Bernoulli variables.

The proof uses the adaptive random-rotation argument of Arjevani et al. (2023, Appendix B.1.2, especially Lemmas 13–14). Lemma 14 gives the required conditional rotational invariance, and the proof of Lemma 13 combines it with spherical concentration. Lemma 4.10 extends the conditional law from a fixed number of initial columns to the random number used here. It remains to verify the required dependence of the complete bilevel oracle response on the initial frame columns.

For the present hard instance, the objects in Lemma 4.11 are defined as follows. At call tt, the public query descriptor is

𝒂t=(𝒙t,𝒛t,𝒗t)∈𝖣≔ℝd×ℝd×ℝ2,\bm{a}_{t}=(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{z}_{t},\bm{v}_{t})\in\mathsf{D}\coloneqq\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{2},

and the associated vector is

𝒓t=ρR​(𝒛t)η.\bm{r}_{t}=\frac{\rho_{R}(\bm{z}_{t})}{\eta}.

The complete oracle response is

𝒀t=(∇f^𝑼κ​(𝒙t,𝒛t,𝒗t),∇g^𝑼κ​(𝒙t,𝒛t,𝒗t,ξt))∈𝖸≔ℝ2​d+2×ℝ2​d+2,\bm{Y}_{t}=\left(\nabla\widehat{f}_{\bm{U}}^{\kappa}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{z}_{t},\bm{v}_{t}),\nabla\widehat{g}_{\bm{U}}^{\kappa}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{z}_{t},\bm{v}_{t};\xi_{t})\right)\in\mathsf{Y}\coloneqq\mathbb{R}^{2d+2}\times\mathbb{R}^{2d+2},

where f^𝑼κ=f𝑼κ\widehat{f}_{\bm{U}}^{\kappa}=f_{\bm{U}}^{\kappa}. The original transcript 𝒯t−1\mathcal{T}_{t-1} consists only of the query-response pairs observed before call tt. The algorithm’s complete pre-query information is

ℱt−1=σ⁡(ωalg,𝒯t−1),\mathscr{F}_{t-1}=\sigma\bigl(\omega_{\rm alg},\mathcal{T}_{t-1}\bigr),

as in (3.3). Since R=230​η​TR=230\eta\sqrt{T}, and ‖ρR​(𝒛t)‖≤R\|\rho_{R}(\bm{z}_{t})\|\leq R, the associated vector satisfies

‖𝒓t‖=‖ρR​(𝒛t)‖η≤Rη=230​T,\|\bm{r}_{t}\|=\frac{\|\rho_{R}(\bm{z}_{t})\|}{\eta}\leq\frac{R}{\eta}=230\sqrt{T},

so the norm condition in Lemma 4.11 is satisfied. Moreover,

prog1/4⁡(𝑼⊤​𝒓t)=progη/4⁡(𝑼⊤​ρR​(𝒛t)).\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}(\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{r}_{t})=\operatorname{prog}_{\eta/4}\bigl(\bm{U}^{\top}\rho_{R}(\bm{z}_{t})\bigr).

At call tt, the number of initial frame columns is ℓ=Lt−1\ell=L_{t-1}, and the bit bb is the realized Bernoulli sample ξt\xi_{t}. Lemma 4.12 below constructs the maps Mt,ℓ(0)M_{t,\ell}^{(0)} and Mt,ℓ(1)M_{t,\ell}^{(1)}: the map for ξt=0\xi_{t}=0 uses only 𝒖1,…,𝒖ℓ\bm{u}_{1},\ldots,\bm{u}_{\ell}, whereas the map for ξt=1\xi_{t}=1 uses only 𝒖1,…,𝒖min⁡{T,ℓ+1}\bm{u}_{1},\ldots,\bm{u}_{\min\{T,\ell+1\}}.

Finally, if 𝒙^N𝖠\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}} is the algorithm’s output, the additional output vector is

𝒓N+1=ρR​(κ​𝒙^N𝖠)η.\bm{r}_{N+1}=\frac{\rho_{R}(\kappa\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}})}{\eta}.

The factor κ​𝒙^N𝖠\kappa\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}} appears because the lower-level solution satisfies 𝒛∗​(𝒙^N𝖠)=κ​𝒙^N𝖠\bm{z}^{*}(\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}})=\kappa\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}}, and the hyper-objective evaluates the chain at this lower solution.

4.5.2 Probability–pp Zero-chain Property

In the following lemma, we verify that the complete joint oracle response satisfies the response-dependence condition of Lemma 4.11, including at the threshold points of the soft indicators. Its proof is given in Appendix C.3.

Lemma 4.12.

Fix a query (𝐱,𝐳,𝐯)(\bm{x},\bm{z},\bm{v}), and write

𝒒=𝒒𝑼​(𝒛)=𝑼⊤​ρR​(𝒛).\bm{q}=\bm{q}_{\bm{U}}(\bm{z})=\bm{U}^{\top}\rho_{R}(\bm{z}). (81)

For every fixed ℓ∈{0,…,T}\ell\in\{0,\ldots,T\}, there are Borel maps Mℓ(0)M_{\ell}^{(0)} and Mℓ(1)M_{\ell}^{(1)}, depending only on the public query and respectively on

𝒖1,…,𝒖ℓand𝒖1,…,𝒖min⁡{T,ℓ+1},\bm{u}_{1},\ldots,\bm{u}_{\ell}\quad\text{and}\quad\bm{u}_{1},\ldots,\bm{u}_{\min\{T,\ell+1\}},

such that, whenever

progη/4⁡(𝒒)≤ℓ,\operatorname{prog}_{\eta/4}(\bm{q})\leq\ell, (82)

the joint upper-lower oracle response with sample bit ξ=b\xi=b is exactly Mℓ(b)M_{\ell}^{(b)}. In particular, these maps do not take the random progress index progη/4⁡(𝐪)\operatorname{prog}_{\eta/4}(\bm{q}) as an argument. They verify the response-dependence condition (75)–(77).

4.5.3 Lower Bound on Oracle Calls

Combining Lemmas 4.11 and Lemma 4.12 with the Bernoulli success-count estimate (70) gives the following progress estimate. Its proof is given in Appendix C.4.

Proposition 4.13.

Fix 𝖠∈𝒜N𝒮​ℱ​𝒪​(d,d+2)\mathsf{A}\in\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\mathcal{SFO}}(d,d+2), and let 𝐱^N𝖠\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}} be its output after NN calls to the oracle (38). Set SN=∑t=1NξtS_{N}=\sum_{t=1}^{N}\xi_{t}. If

N≤T8​pN\leq\frac{T}{8p} (83)

and

d≥T+CH​(2302​T)​(N+1)​log⁡(16​(N+1)2​T),d\geq T+C_{\rm H}(230^{2}T)(N+1)\log(16(N+1)^{2}T), (84)

then, jointly over 𝐔\bm{U}, the algorithm’s private randomness, and the fresh oracle samples,

ℙ⁡(progη/4⁡(𝑼⊤​ρR​(κ​𝒙^N𝖠))<T)≥34.\mathbb{P}\left(\operatorname{prog}_{\eta/4}\!\left(\bm{U}^{\top}\rho_{R}(\kappa\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}})\right)<T\right)\geq\frac{3}{4}. (85)
Remark 4.14.

The dimension condition (84) ensures, through spherical concentration, that an adaptive query has a small projection onto each remaining frame column with high probability. It does not add a factor to the oracle lower bound. After the call budget NN is fixed, the proof chooses a sufficiently large finite dimension dd. The conclusion then holds for every 𝖠∈𝒜N𝒮​ℱ​𝒪​(d,d+2)\mathsf{A}\in\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\mathcal{SFO}}(d,d+2), although the final deterministic frame and hence the hard instance may depend on 𝖠\mathsf{A}. The oracle complexity is determined by T/pT/p; the dimension condition is used only in the random-rotation argument.

Proposition 4.13 implies that, for N≤T/(8​p)N\leq T/(8p), the rotated chain coordinates at the output have progress below TT with probability at least 3/43/4. Lemma 4.9 then gives a hypergradient above the target accuracy on this event. Appendix E combines these estimates and proves Theorem 4.1.

5 Conclusion and Future Work

We established the stochastic first-order lower bound

Ω⁡(Δ​κy2ϵ2​max⁡{1,σ2​κy6ϵ4})\Omega\!\left(\frac{\Delta\kappa_{y}^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\max\left\{1,\frac{\sigma^{2}\kappa_{y}^{6}}{\epsilon^{4}}\right\}\right)

for smooth NC-SC bilevel optimization over arbitrary adaptive randomized first-order algorithms. In the noise-dominated regime, this becomes Ω⁡(Δ​σ2​κy8​ϵ−6)\Omega(\Delta\sigma^{2}\kappa_{y}^{8}\epsilon^{-6}), showing that the ϵ−6\epsilon^{-6} dependence of the best-known first-order upper bounds (Chen et al., 2025b; Gu et al., 2026) is information-theoretically unavoidable under the bounded-variance 𝒮​ℱ​𝒪\mathcal{SFO} model. The optimal dependence on the condition number remains open, however, in view of the upper bound 𝒪~​(κ¯y11​ϵ−6)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(\bar{\kappa}_{y}^{11}\epsilon^{-6}\right) of Chen et al. (2025b). Another interesting direction is to establish lower bounds in a fixed ambient dimension, rather than allowing the dimension to grow with the target accuracy.

AI Disclosure

The hard-instance construction and its presentation were refined through iterative collaboration with OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. The authors supplied the model with an independently developed proof draft targeting an ϵ−6\epsilon^{-6} lower bound, motivated by their unpublished upper-bound result showing that ϵ−4\epsilon^{-4} complexity bound is attainable when the lower-level objective is quadratic or satisfies an averaged stochastic smoothness condition, but not necessarily for the general problem class. The authors independently checked all mathematical arguments and take full responsibility for the content of the paper. An accompanying Lean formalization, developed with assistance from Codex and available at https://github.com/Wu-Qilong/Lower-Bounds-for-Nonconvex-Strongly-Convex-Bilevel-Optimization, provides machine-checked verification of the lower-bound argument.

B.1 Proof of Lemma 4.4

Proof.

Write

s⁡(𝒛)=1+‖𝒛‖2/R2,α⁡(𝒛)=s​(𝒛)−1,𝒓=ρR​(𝒛)=𝒛/s⁡(𝒛).s(\bm{z})=\sqrt{1+\left\lVert\bm{z}\right\rVert^{2}/R^{2}},\qquad\alpha(\bm{z})=s(\bm{z})^{-1},\qquad\bm{r}=\rho_{R}(\bm{z})=\bm{z}/s(\bm{z}).

D​ρR​(𝒛)=α​𝑰−α3R2​𝒛​𝒛⊤=𝑰s⁡(𝒛)−𝒓​𝒓⊤R2​s​(𝒛).D\rho_{R}(\bm{z})=\alpha\bm{I}-\frac{\alpha^{3}}{R^{2}}\bm{z}\bm{z}^{\top}=\frac{\bm{I}}{s(\bm{z})}-\frac{\bm{r}\bm{r}^{\top}}{R^{2}s(\bm{z})}. (98)

The two distinct eigenvalues of this symmetric matrix are in [0,1][0,1], so ‖D​ρR​(𝒛)‖op≤1\left\lVert D\rho_{R}(\bm{z})\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 1. Indeed, if 𝒛=0\bm{z}=0, then α⁡(𝟎)=1\alpha(\bm{0})=1, and

D​ρR​(𝟎)=𝑰.D\rho_{R}(\bm{0})=\bm{I}.

Consequently,

‖D​ρR​(𝟎)‖op=‖𝑰‖op=1.\|D\rho_{R}(\bm{0})\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|\bm{I}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=1.

Suppose now that 𝒛≠0\bm{z}\neq 0, and define the unit vector 𝒆=𝒛‖𝒛‖\bm{e}=\frac{\bm{z}}{\|\bm{z}\|}. Every vector 𝒉∈ℝd\bm{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} has the orthogonal decomposition

𝒉=𝒉∥+𝒉⟂,𝒉∥=⟨𝒆,𝒉⟩​𝒆,𝒉⟂=𝒉−⟨𝒆,𝒉⟩​𝒆,\bm{h}=\bm{h}_{\parallel}+\bm{h}_{\perp},\qquad\bm{h}_{\parallel}=\langle\bm{e},\bm{h}\rangle\bm{e},\qquad\bm{h}_{\perp}=\bm{h}-\langle\bm{e},\bm{h}\rangle\bm{e},

where

𝒉∥∈span⁡{𝒛},⟨𝒛,𝒉⟂⟩=0.\bm{h}_{\parallel}\in\operatorname{span}\{\bm{z}\},\qquad\langle\bm{z},\bm{h}_{\perp}\rangle=0.

We first examine the action of D​ρR​(𝒛)D\rho_{R}(\bm{z}) on the orthogonal subspace 𝒛⟂\bm{z}^{\perp}. Since ⟨𝒛,𝒉⟂⟩=0\langle\bm{z},\bm{h}_{\perp}\rangle=0,

D​ρR​(𝒛)​𝒉⟂=α⁡(𝒛)​𝒉⟂−α​(𝒛)3R2​𝒛​𝒛⊤​𝒉⟂=α⁡(𝒛)​𝒉⟂.\displaystyle D\rho_{R}(\bm{z})\bm{h}_{\perp}=\alpha(\bm{z})\bm{h}_{\perp}-\frac{\alpha(\bm{z})^{3}}{R^{2}}\bm{z}\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{h}_{\perp}=\alpha(\bm{z})\bm{h}_{\perp}. (99)

Appendix C Proofs for Section 4.5

C.1 Proof of Lemma 4.10

Proof.

For a fixed number ℓ\ell of initial frame columns, disintegration of Haar measure with respect to these columns gives the completion kernel 𝖪ℓ\mathsf{K}_{\ell}; this is the conditional-rotation statement used in Arjevani et al. (2023, Lemma 14). To pass to the random index JJ, test the displayed candidate conditional expectation against a bounded ℋJ\mathscr{H}_{J}-measurable function. On the stratum {J=ℓ}\{J=\ell\}, that test function is a Borel function of (Z,𝑼≤ℓ)(Z,\bm{U}_{\leq\ell}). The event {J=ℓ}\{J=\ell\} is measurable with respect to ZZ and is therefore independent of 𝑼\bm{U}. Applying the conditional Haar disintegration on this stratum gives the conditional-expectation identity. The defining property of a Borel probability kernel also makes the kernel integral Borel in (Z,𝑼≤ℓ)(Z,\bm{U}_{\leq\ell}), so the displayed candidate is ℋJ\mathscr{H}_{J}-measurable. Summing over the finite partition {J=0},…,{J=T}\{J=0\},\ldots,\{J=T\} proves the formula. The marginal statement follows from rotational invariance of the completion kernel. ∎

C.2 Proof of Lemma 4.11

Proof.

We use the adaptive random-rotation argument of Arjevani et al. (2023, Appendix B.1.2, especially Lemmas 13–14). Lemma 14 provides the relevant conditional rotational invariance, while the proof of Lemma 13 combines it with the standard spherical-cap estimate. The coupled-transcript argument below is our specialization of these ingredients and is not a verbatim restatement of either cited lemma.

Step 1: augment the transcript with the first recorded frame columns. For the purpose of the conditional-Haar argument, after call tt we record the Bernoulli bits ξ1,…,ξt\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{t} and the first LtL_{t} columns 𝒖1,…,𝒖Lt\bm{u}_{1},\ldots,\bm{u}_{L_{t}} in an augmented transcript. Let 𝒯torig\mathcal{T}_{t}^{\rm orig} denote the transcript actually observed by the original procedure, and define

𝒯t=(𝒯torig,ξ1,…,ξt,𝒖1,…,𝒖Lt).\mathcal{T}_{t}=\bigl(\mathcal{T}_{t}^{\rm orig},\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{t},\bm{u}_{1},\ldots,\bm{u}_{L_{t}}\bigr).

The additional transcript entries are auxiliary variables used only in the proof; they are not additional oracle observations available to the original procedure. Throughout the remainder of this proof, 𝒯torig\mathcal{T}_{t}^{\rm orig} denotes the original query-response transcript, whereas 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} denotes the augmented transcript defined above.

For the algorithm fixed in Proposition 4.13, the original query and output rules are induced by Queryt𝖠\operatorname{Query}_{t}^{\mathsf{A}} and OutputN𝖠\operatorname{Output}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}} from Definition 3.3. The query descriptor and its associated vector are obtained from the algorithmic query through the Borel map

(𝒙t,𝒛t,𝒗t)⟼((𝒙t,𝒛t,𝒗t),ρR​(𝒛t)η).(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{z}_{t},\bm{v}_{t})\longmapsto\left((\bm{x}_{t},\bm{z}_{t},\bm{v}_{t}),\frac{\rho_{R}(\bm{z}_{t})}{\eta}\right).

Let πtorig\pi_{t}^{\rm orig} denote the canonical projection onto the original transcript component, so that

πtorig​(𝒯t)=𝒯torig.\pi_{t}^{\rm orig}(\mathcal{T}_{t})=\mathcal{T}_{t}^{\rm orig}.

The original query rule is extended to the augmented transcript space by

Querytaug⁡(ωalg,𝒯t−1)=Querytorig⁡(ωalg,πt−1orig​(𝒯t−1)),\operatorname{Query}_{t}^{\rm aug}(\omega_{\rm alg},\mathcal{T}_{t-1})=\operatorname{Query}_{t}^{\rm orig}\bigl(\omega_{\rm alg},\pi_{t-1}^{\rm orig}(\mathcal{T}_{t-1})\bigr),

and the output rule is extended by

Outputaug⁡(ωalg,𝒯N)=Outputorig⁡(ωalg,πNorig​(𝒯N)).\operatorname{Output}^{\rm aug}(\omega_{\rm alg},\mathcal{T}_{N})=\operatorname{Output}^{\rm orig}\bigl(\omega_{\rm alg},\pi_{N}^{\rm orig}(\mathcal{T}_{N})\bigr).

Thus the additional Bernoulli bits and frame columns are available for the measurability argument but do not affect the actual queries or the final output of the original procedure.

For uniform notation, let JtJ_{t} be the number of recorded frame columns associated with each of the n=N+1n=N+1 vectors, and set

Jt={Lt−1,1≤t≤N,LN,t=n=N+1.J_{t}=\begin{cases}L_{t-1},&1\leq t\leq N,\\ L_{N},&t=n=N+1.\end{cases} (137)

Thus JtJ_{t} is the number of columns recorded in the augmented transcript when 𝒓t\bm{r}_{t} is formed. In particular, the additional output vector 𝒓n=𝒓N+1\bm{r}_{n}=\bm{r}_{N+1} is assigned Jn=LNJ_{n}=L_{N}, because it receives no new Bernoulli draw or oracle response.

Step 2: construct a coupled transcript with the required measurability. Let ωalg\omega_{\rm alg} be the random seed of the algorithm from Definition 3.3. By construction, it is independent of 𝑼\bm{U} and of ξ1,…,ξN\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{N}. After conditioning on ωalg\omega_{\rm alg}, the procedure’s query and output rules are Borel deterministic maps of their transcripts. We construct recursively an augmented coupled transcript 𝒯~t\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}_{t}, whose original query-response component is

𝒯~torig=πtorig​(𝒯~t),\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}_{t}^{\rm orig}=\pi_{t}^{\rm orig}(\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}_{t}), (138)

together with coupled query descriptors 𝒂~t\widetilde{\bm{a}}_{t}, coupled vectors 𝒓~t\widetilde{\bm{r}}_{t}, and coupled responses 𝒀~t\widetilde{\bm{Y}}_{t}.

Start with the same original and augmented initial transcripts:

ℙ⁡(ℬt,s,j)≤δn2​Tfor every fixed ​(t,s,j).\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{B}_{t,s,j})\leq\frac{\delta}{n^{2}T}\qquad\text{for every fixed }(t,s,j). (166)

At call tt, take ℓ=Lt−1\ell=L_{t-1}. On the geometric event progη/4⁡(𝑼⊤​ρR​(𝒛t))≤Lt−1\operatorname{prog}_{\eta/4}(\bm{U}^{\top}\rho_{R}(\bm{z}_{t}))\leq L_{t-1}, the preceding identities show that the actual joint response satisfies

C.4 Proof of Proposition 4.13

Proof.

Step 1: associate a bounded vector with each query. At call tt, let 𝒂t=(𝒙t,𝒛t,𝒗t)\bm{a}_{t}=(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{z}_{t},\bm{v}_{t}) be the point selected by the algorithm and define

𝒓t=ρR​(𝒛t)η.\bm{r}_{t}=\frac{\rho_{R}(\bm{z}_{t})}{\eta}. (180)

The soft projection satisfies

‖ρR​(𝒛t)‖<R=230​η​T.\left\lVert\rho_{R}(\bm{z}_{t})\right\rVert<R=230\eta\sqrt{T}.

Therefore

‖𝒓t‖=‖ρR​(𝒛t)‖η≤Rη=230​T.\left\lVert\bm{r}_{t}\right\rVert=\frac{\left\lVert\rho_{R}(\bm{z}_{t})\right\rVert}{\eta}\leq\frac{R}{\eta}=230\sqrt{T}. (181)

The construction has T≥1T\geq 1, so R=230​η​T>ηR=230\eta\sqrt{T}>\eta. Moreover, (60) gives 0<p≤10<p\leq 1, the dimension condition implies d≥Td\geq T, and (181) gives the required norm bound. Thus the basic parameter and norm conditions of Lemma 4.11 are satisfied.

Step 2: include an output that was never queried. The algorithm may return a point 𝒙^N𝖠\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}} at which it never called the oracle. The hyper-objective at 𝒙^N𝖠\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}} evaluates the rotated zero-chain at the lower level solution

𝒛∗​(𝒙^N𝖠)=κ​𝒙^N𝖠.\bm{z}^{*}(\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}})=\kappa\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}}.

Accordingly, append the additional output vector

𝒓N+1=ρR​(κ​𝒙^N𝖠)η.\bm{r}_{N+1}=\frac{\rho_{R}(\kappa\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}})}{\eta}. (182)

It obeys the same norm bound as (181). No oracle response is returned, so this additional vector provides no additional oracle information and does not change LNL_{N}.

Step 3: apply the adaptive Haar lemma. Lemma 4.12 verifies the required response-dependence condition. Choose δ=1/8\delta=1/8. Substituting R2=2302​η2​TR^{2}=230^{2}\eta^{2}T and 2​(N+1)2​T/δ=16​(N+1)2​T2(N+1)^{2}T/\delta=16(N+1)^{2}T into (78) gives exactly (84). Hence, with probability at least 7/87/8,

prog1/4⁡(𝑼⊤​ρR​(κ​𝒙^N𝖠)η)≤LN=min⁡{T,SN}.\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}\!\left(\bm{U}^{\top}\frac{\rho_{R}(\kappa\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}})}{\eta}\right)\leq L_{N}=\min\{T,S_{N}\}. (183)

For every coordinate jj, because η>0\eta>0,

|[𝑼⊤​ρR​(κ​𝒙^N𝖠)/η]j|>14\left\lvert\left[\bm{U}^{\top}\rho_{R}(\kappa\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}})/\eta\right]_{j}\right\rvert>\frac{1}{4}

holds if and only if

|[𝑼⊤​ρR​(κ​𝒙^N𝖠)]j|>η4.\left\lvert\left[\bm{U}^{\top}\rho_{R}(\kappa\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}})\right]_{j}\right\rvert>\frac{\eta}{4}.

Therefore

prog1/4⁡(𝑼⊤​ρR​(κ​𝒙^N𝖠)η)=progη/4⁡(𝑼⊤​ρR​(κ​𝒙^N𝖠)).\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}\!\left(\bm{U}^{\top}\frac{\rho_{R}(\kappa\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}})}{\eta}\right)=\operatorname{prog}_{\eta/4}\!\left(\bm{U}^{\top}\rho_{R}(\kappa\widehat{\bm{x}}_{N}^{\mathsf{A}})\right). (184)

Step 4: fewer than TT successes occur with high probability. Freshness gives

𝔼⁡[ξt∣ℱt−1]=p.\mathbb{E}[\xi_{t}\mid\mathscr{F}_{t-1}]=p.

Using the tower property and summing over the calls,

𝔼​SN=∑t=1N𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[ξt∣ℱt−1]]=N​p.\mathbb{E}S_{N}=\sum_{t=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbb{E}[\xi_{t}\mid\mathscr{F}_{t-1}]\right]=Np. (185)
